We treat yards all over town, from the neighborhoods near Prospector Park and Silly Mountain Park to the larger desert lots off the Apache Trail toward Goldfield Ghost Town. You can see everything we do locally on our Apache Junction weed control page.

We also serve the neighboring communities of Gold Canyon, Mesa, Queen Creek, San Tan Valley and Florence. Whether you have a few stubborn weeds or a whole yard that turned green after the rain, we can take a look and tell you what will work.

Frequently Asked Questions About DIY Weed Killer

What is the strongest homemade weed killer?

Recipes that use horticultural vinegar instead of kitchen vinegar burn weeds fastest, but they are also the most dangerous to skin and eyes. Even the strongest vinegar or soap mix only kills the leaves and stems it touches, so perennial weeds like Bermuda grass and nutsedge usually regrow from their roots.

Does vinegar kill weeds permanently?

No. Vinegar burns the leaves but does not move into the roots. Small annual weeds may die, but established and perennial weeds usually come back, and new seeds keep sprouting after each rain.

How long does salt stay in the soil?

It depends on the soil and how much water moves through it. In our dry climate, there is less rain to flush salt down, so it can linger near the surface. That is why we only suggest salt on hardscape, well away from plants.

Is a DIY weed killer safer than a registered product?

Not automatically. Strong vinegar is corrosive, and salt can damage soil and plants. A registered product has label directions for safe use, including when people and pets can go back on the treated area. A homemade mix has no tested directions at all.

Can I use a homemade weed killer in a gravel yard?

Vinegar on a few small weeds in gravel is fine. Avoid salt in gravel beds that have plants or trees, because it can spread through the soil to their roots. For a whole gravel yard, a pre-emergent and post-emergent plan is far less work.

How do I get a weed treatment scheduled in Apache Junction?

Call us at (480) 422-8388 or request service online. We'll ask what weeds you are seeing and set up a visit.

does-borax-and-sugar-kill-ants-what-san-.title: Does Borax and Sugar Kill Ants? What San Tan Valley Homeowners Should Know Before Mixing a Homemade Ant Bait
does-borax-and-sugar-kill-ants-what-san-.excerpt: Borax and sugar slowly kill sweet-feeding ants but rarely a whole colony, and do little against fire ants. What San Tan Valley homeowners should know.
does-borax-and-sugar-kill-ants-what-san-.content:
Yes, borax and sugar can kill ants, but only some ants and only slowly. The sugar draws in sweet-feeding workers, and the borax works as a stomach poison they carry back to the nest. In San Tan Valley it often thins out a kitchen trail of small sugar ants, but it rarely finishes a large outdoor colony, and it does little against fire ants or harvester ants. If the trail is back in two weeks, call us at (480) 422-8388.

We get this question a lot in 85140 and 85143. Someone finds a line of tiny ants running from the patio slider to the pantry, searches for a fix, and ends up with a jar lid of borax and sugar under the sink. Sometimes that works. Often the ants vanish for a week and come right back. This guide explains why, how a borax bait is supposed to work, where it fails in a desert yard on the edge of the San Tan Mountains, and when our ant control in San Tan Valley is the faster route.

How Does a Borax and Sugar Ant Bait Work?

A bait is not a spray. It is meant to be eaten, shared and spread through the colony. Here is the chain that has to happen:

  1. A foraging worker finds the sugar and eats it.
  2. She walks back to the nest with it in her crop (a storage stomach).
  3. She shares it with other workers, the larvae and the queen.
  4. The borax slowly damages the gut of every ant that ate it.

Borax is a sodium borate salt, a close relative of boric acid. The National Pesticide Information Center explains that boric acid can kill insects when they eat it, because it disrupts their stomach and can affect their nervous system. You can read the NPIC boric acid fact sheet for the details.

The key word is slow. University of California IPM puts it plainly in its ant pest note: a bait has to be slow-acting so workers are not killed before they get back to the nest. If the mix kills the foragers on the spot, the queen never gets a bite and the colony keeps producing new workers.

Why Does a Homemade Borax Bait Work Sometimes and Fail Other Times?

Most recipes online mix roughly one part borax with three parts sugar, sometimes with water to make a syrup. The trouble is that a kitchen recipe has no way to control the dose. A few things decide whether it works in your house.

Is the mix too strong?

Too much borax and the ants die near the bait or refuse it. You see dead ants around the lid and feel good, but the colony is untouched. This is the most common reason a homemade bait "worked for a few days."

Is the mix too weak or drying out?

San Tan Valley air is dry for most of the year. A syrup bait left on a piece of cardboard can crust over in a day or two, and ants stop feeding on it. Wet baits need to be refreshed often.

Are these ants even eating sugar right now?

Colonies change what they want. A colony raising lots of larvae may switch to protein and grease for a while. During that stretch a sugar bait gets ignored, even by ants that loved it last month.

Is the colony too big?

Some common ants live in huge colonies with many queens spread across a yard. A jar lid of bait can kill thousands of workers and still never reach most of the queens.

Which San Tan Valley Ants Will Take a Sugar Bait?

Identification matters more than the recipe. UC IPM's household ant table lists what most of these species feed on (harvester ants, which UC IPM covers separately, collect seeds), and it lines up with what we find on calls from Johnson Ranch to Pecan Creek.

Ant Where we find it Main foods Will a borax and sugar bait help?
Argentine ant (small, dull brown) Kitchens, bathrooms, along irrigated beds Sweets, sometimes proteins Can reduce the trail, but large multi-queen colonies usually bounce back
Pavement ant (dark brown to black) Slab cracks, patios, under pavers Sweets, proteins, grease Hit or miss, depending on what the colony wants that week
Southern fire ant (amber and dark, stings) Irrigated lawns, garden beds, around AC pads Proteins and sweets Poor choice; a stinging colony in the yard needs a targeted treatment
Harvester ant (large, red, big cleared mound) Open desert lots and gravel yards Seeds No; they are not after sugar
Carpenter ant (large, black or red and black) Damp wood, fence posts, eaves Sweets May take it, but you also need to find the nest in the wood

If you are not sure what you have, a few ants taped to an index card are enough for our technicians to identify them. Flying "ants" in a house are a separate question. They are sometimes termite swarmers, which we cover in our guide to signs of white ants in a house.

Is Borax Safe Around Kids and Pets?

Borax sounds harmless because it sits in the laundry aisle, but it is still a pesticide when you use it this way. NPIC notes that borax can irritate skin and can be corrosive to the eyes, that people who swallowed boric acid have had nausea, vomiting and stomach pain, and that infants are more sensitive. Animals can show signs of poisoning within two hours of eating it.

A sweet bait is exactly the kind of thing a toddler or a dog will go after. If you try it:

  • Put the bait inside a closed container with small holes, not on an open lid.
  • Keep it behind appliances, inside cabinets kids cannot open, or outdoors where pets cannot reach.
  • Wear gloves when mixing and wash your hands before eating.
  • Label the container clearly and throw out leftovers.
  • If a child or pet eats some, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 or your veterinarian right away.

Store-bought bait stations use the same idea in a sealed, tested package with label directions. For most families that is a safer starting point than a homemade mix.

Why Do Ants Keep Coming Back in San Tan Valley Homes?

San Tan Valley is mostly newer homes built on what was open desert a few years ago. That matters for ants.

  • Disturbed soil. Grading and construction break up native colonies, and the survivors move into fresh landscape rock, block walls and slab edges. Homes in Bella Vista Farms and Copper Basin that back onto empty lots see this most.
  • Irrigation. Drip lines and turf watering create damp, cool soil in a dry landscape. Ants follow the water, especially in May and June before the monsoon.
  • Monsoon rain. Heavy storms flood nests, and colonies move uphill, which often means under your slab or along the foundation.
  • Slab cracks and slider tracks. Most trails we trace in 85143 enter at the patio door threshold, a garage expansion joint or a pipe opening under the sink.

Killing the trail inside does not change any of that. The colony outside keeps sending scouts until the source is treated.

What Should You Do Before You Mix a Homemade Ant Killer?

A few minutes of prep makes any bait, homemade or store-bought, work better.

  1. Do not spray the trail first. A repellent spray scatters the colony and teaches ants to avoid the area. Baits need ants that are actively feeding. Our post on why store-bought ant sprays fail goes deeper on this.
  2. Remove the competition. Wipe counters, seal the sugar and cereal, rinse recycling and fix the dripping hose bib. Ants will not work hard for bait if there is free food nearby.
  3. Follow the trail. Watch where the line goes at dusk. Bait near the entry point or the outdoor nest, not in the middle of the counter.
  4. Give it time. More ants for the first day or two is normal with a bait. Judge results after about a week.
  5. Know when to stop. If ants are still trailing after two weeks of steady baiting, the colony is too big, too spread out or not eating sugar.

Our guide to repelling sugar ants in the kitchen covers the clean-up side in more detail. If you have tried everything and the same trail returns, our guide to why sugar ants keep coming back explains the colony biology behind it.

When Is It Time to Call a Professional for Ants?

Call us when any of these are true:

  • The trail comes back after two weeks of baiting.
  • You see ants in more than one room, or coming out of walls or outlets.
  • Ants are stinging kids or pets in the yard. For stinging ants, see our Pinal County fire ant guide.
  • You find large ants in wood, or winged insects coming out of the slab.
  • You have a baby, a crawling toddler or a curious dog and do not want bait in the house.

On an ant visit our technicians identify the species, trace the trail to the entry point, place professional baits where the ants are feeding and treat the outside perimeter so new scouts do not move in. We also look for the scorpions and spiders that follow ants into San Tan Valley yards, and we can add scorpion control in San Tan Valley on the same visit. You can see everything we treat on our San Tan Valley pest control page.

Do We Treat Ants Near San Tan Valley Too?

Yes. Our Apache Junction office covers the whole southeast Valley and Pinal County, including ant control in Queen Creek, pest control in Florence, Gilbert, Apache Junction and Mesa. If you live in Skyline Ranch, Johnson Ranch, Pecan Creek, Copper Basin or anywhere off Hunt Highway and Bella Vista Road, you are in our regular service area. Learn more about the area on our San Tan Valley page.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long does borax and sugar take to kill ants?

If it works, you usually see fewer ants within several days to a week. A bait is meant to be slow so workers can carry it back to the nest. Ants that die right at the bait are a sign the mix is too strong.

Does borax kill the queen ant?

It can, but only if workers carry enough of it back and share it before they die. In large, multi-queen colonies like Argentine ants, a homemade bait rarely reaches every queen, which is why trails come back.

Why are there more ants after I put out borax and sugar?

That is normal for the first day or two. Scouts recruit more workers to the food. Leave the bait alone and keep it fresh. If the numbers have not dropped after a week, the bait is not working for that colony.

Will borax and sugar kill fire ants?

It is a poor choice for fire ants. They nest in the yard, feed on protein as well as sweets, and sting when disturbed. A stinging colony near where kids or pets play is worth a targeted professional treatment.

Is a borax ant killer safe to use if I have a dog?

Only if the dog truly cannot reach it. A sweet bait attracts pets, and NPIC notes animals can show signs of poisoning within two hours of eating boric acid. Use a closed station placed out of reach, or skip it and call us.

How do I schedule ant control in San Tan Valley?

Call us at (480) 422-8388 or request service online. Tell us where you are seeing the ants, and we will set up a visit.

what-do-cockroaches-look-like-a-chandler.title: What Do Cockroaches Look Like? A Chandler Homeowner's Guide to Identifying Arizona Roaches
what-do-cockroaches-look-like-a-chandler.excerpt: German roaches are half-inch and tan with two stripes; American roaches are 2-inch and reddish. How Chandler homeowners can identify every Arizona roach.
what-do-cockroaches-look-like-a-chandler.content:
Most cockroaches in Chandler homes are flat, oval, brown insects with six spiny legs and long, thread-like antennae, and the species tell themselves apart by size and markings. A half-inch tan roach with two dark stripes behind its head is a German cockroach. A reddish-brown one close to two inches long is an American cockroach. A dark one about an inch long is usually a Turkestan or Oriental roach. Seeing them indoors? Call (480) 422-8388.

Identification matters more than most people think. The roach you find decides where it came from, whether it is breeding inside your walls or just wandering in from the yard, and what treatment will actually work. Over the years our technicians have learned to read these insects quickly in houses from the 85224 neighborhoods north of the Loop 202 down to Ocotillo and Sun Groves in 85248 and 85249. This guide walks you through what each Arizona cockroach looks like, how to tell the babies and egg cases apart, which insects get mistaken for roaches, and when it is time for cockroach control in Chandler.

What Does a Cockroach Look Like Up Close?

Every cockroach shares the same basic body plan, whatever the species. If the insect in your kitchen has most of these features, it is a roach:

  • A flattened, oval body that lets it slide under a door sweep or into a crack about as thick as a coin.
  • A shield over the head (the pronotum). From above you often cannot see the head at all. The markings on this shield are the quickest way to name the species.
  • Long, whip-like antennae, often as long as the body or longer, that constantly sweep side to side.
  • Six legs covered in small spines, built for running, not jumping.
  • Two short "tail" feelers (cerci) at the tip of the abdomen.
  • Leathery wings on adults of most species, folded flat over the back. Some females have only short wing pads.

Color runs from pale tan to almost black. Shine, size and stripes do the rest of the work, as the table below shows.

Which Cockroaches Live in Chandler, and How Do You Tell Them Apart?

Five species account for nearly every roach call we get in the East Valley. University of California IPM's cockroach pest note describes the same group for the desert Southwest.

SpeciesAdult sizeColor and markingsWhere we usually find it
German cockroachAbout 1/2 inchLight tan, two dark parallel stripes on the shield behind the headInside: kitchens, dishwashers, under sinks, bathrooms
American cockroachAbout 1.5 to 2 inchesReddish-brown, pale yellowish band around the edge of the head shieldSewer lines, drains, utility boxes, block wall caps
Turkestan cockroachAbout 1 inchMales slim and tan with cream edges on the wings; females dark brown to black with short wing pads and cream marks near the headIrrigation boxes, meter boxes, cracks in patios, gravel beds
Oriental cockroachAbout 1 inchShiny dark brown to black; males have wings that stop short of the tail, females only wing padsDamp, cool spots: drains, crawl spaces, water meter boxes
Brown-banded cockroachAbout 1/2 inchLight brown with two pale bands across the wings and abdomenWarm, high spots indoors: behind pictures, inside electronics, upper cabinets

The two you are most likely to see in a Chandler home are the German roach inside and the American or Turkestan roach coming in from outside. Telling them apart is the single most useful thing you can do before calling anyone.

What Does a German Cockroach Look Like?

The German cockroach is small, about the size of a fingernail, and light tan to medium brown. The giveaway is the pair of dark stripes running front to back on the shield behind its head. Adults have wings that cover the whole abdomen, but they almost never fly.

Why German roaches are the ones to worry about

German roaches live their entire lives indoors, breed quickly, and hide in the warm spots around refrigerators, dishwashers, microwaves and the hinges of cabinet doors. Females carry their egg case attached to the abdomen until just before it hatches, which protects the eggs from many sprays. If you see these during the day, the population is usually large. Our guide to getting rid of German cockroaches explains why baits beat bug bombs for this species.

What Does an American Cockroach Look Like?

This is the big one. American cockroaches are reddish-brown, roughly 1.5 to 2 inches long, with a pale, yellowish band around the edge of the head shield that looks like a faint outline. Both sexes have full wings that reach past the tip of the abdomen. They are the roaches people call "sewer roaches," "palmetto bugs" or "water bugs," and they are strong enough to glide off a block wall on a warm night. If one landed on you, our post on whether cockroaches can fly covers that behavior.

In Chandler they live in the municipal sewer and storm system, in irrigation and utility boxes, and in the hollow caps of block walls. They usually come up through floor drains, tub drains, or gaps around plumbing under sinks, especially after summer monsoon storms flush the lines. Our article on water bugs vs cockroaches goes deeper into the drain side of the problem.

What Do Turkestan and Oriental Cockroaches Look Like?

These are the medium-sized outdoor roaches, and in new-build neighborhoods like Fulton Ranch and the communities south of the Santan Freeway they are often the first roach a family sees.

  • Turkestan males are slender, tan to yellowish, with cream-colored stripes along the outer edges of the wings. They are attracted to porch lights and often turn up dead on patios in summer.
  • Turkestan females look like a different insect: dark brown to nearly black, with tiny wing pads and short cream marks near the head. Seeing both "kinds" together is a sign of an outdoor breeding site nearby.
  • Oriental roaches are glossy, dark brown to black, and slow. Males have wings that cover only part of the back; females have just stubs. They need cool, damp places and are less common in the dry heat than Turkestan roaches.

Turkestan roaches have spread across much of the desert Southwest and often replace Oriental roaches where both used to live. Both breed in water meter boxes, irrigation valve boxes, cracks between pavers and under landscape rock.

What Do Baby Cockroaches and Egg Cases Look Like?

Young roaches (nymphs) look like small, wingless adults. They molt several times and grow a little larger each time. They are often what people actually find, and they are the clearest sign that roaches are breeding where you saw them.

Nymphs

  • German nymphs are dark brown to almost black with a single pale stripe down the middle of the back. They are tiny, roughly the size of a grain of rice when they hatch.
  • American nymphs are uniform reddish-brown and grow from about a quarter inch to adult size over many months.
  • Turkestan and Oriental nymphs are dark and shiny and are usually found outside near the adults.

Egg cases (oothecae)

Roach eggs come packed in a hard, bean- or purse-shaped capsule. American and Turkestan egg cases are dark brown and about a third of an inch long, and females glue them in hidden spots. German egg cases are lighter tan and stay attached to the female until hatching. Brown-banded females stick their small cases to the undersides of furniture and shelves. If you find empty capsules in a drawer or behind the stove, you have had a breeding population, not a visitor.

What Bugs Look Like Cockroaches but Aren't?

Plenty of "roach" sightings turn out to be something else. In the desert, these are the common look-alikes:

  1. Ground beetles and darkling beetles. Hard, shiny wing covers that meet in a straight line down the back, short antennae, and a visible head. Darkling beetles (often called stink beetles) raise their rear end when disturbed.
  2. Crickets. Big hind legs built for jumping, and they chirp. Field crickets swarm lights in late summer.
  3. June beetles and fig beetles. Round, heavy, hard-shelled, and clumsy fliers drawn to porch lights.
  4. True water bugs. Aquatic insects with grasping front legs that live in ponds and pools. They are not roaches, though American roaches borrow the name.
  5. Bed bugs. Sometimes mistaken for baby roaches, but bed bugs are flat, round, rust-colored, and have no long antennae or running legs.

A quick check: if it has a hard shell split down the middle and short antennae, it is a beetle. If it has a soft, leathery back, long waving antennae and runs fast for cover, it is a roach.

Why Are You Seeing Cockroaches in Your Chandler Home?

Where and when you see roaches says as much as what they look like. Here is what we usually find behind each pattern in Chandler, AZ homes:

  • Big roaches in bathrooms or the laundry room, mostly at night: American roaches coming up through drains or around unsealed plumbing. More common in the older homes around Downtown Chandler and the 85225 area where lines and slabs have aged.
  • Medium dark roaches on the patio or in the garage: Turkestan roaches breeding in meter boxes, irrigation boxes and gravel beds. Common across 85226, 85248 and 85249.
  • Small tan roaches in the kitchen, even in daylight: German roaches established indoors. These often arrive in grocery boxes, used appliances or moving cartons, and they spread easily between attached units in apartments and townhomes.
  • Dead roaches on their backs in the garage: Usually outdoor species that wandered in and contacted a treated surface.

Roaches also bring scorpions. Bark scorpions feed on small insects, and a yard full of roaches and crickets supports more of them, so roach problems and scorpion control in Chandler are often the same job.

What Should You Do After You Identify the Roach?

Your next step depends on the species:

  1. Take a clear photo from above, with something for scale like a coin. Note where and what time you saw it.
  2. If it is an American roach, check floor drains and tub overflows, put stoppers in unused drains, and look for gaps around pipes under sinks.
  3. If it is a Turkestan or Oriental roach, open your water meter and irrigation boxes and look for activity, pull mulch and rock back from the slab, and switch porch bulbs to yellow LEDs.
  4. If it is a German roach, skip the foggers. They scatter roaches deeper into walls. Clean grease from behind the stove, fix leaks under sinks, and call a professional, because German populations rarely clear up with store products.

Our technicians treat the source, not just the roaches you can see: drains and plumbing gaps for American roaches, outdoor harborage for Turkestan roaches, and targeted gel baits and growth regulators inside for German roaches. That is part of every pest control in Chandler visit. We also serve nearby Gilbert, Mesa, Tempe, Queen Creek and Ahwatukee, and we see the same species across the whole East Valley. You can read about roach elimination in Gilbert or our pest control in Mesa if you are just across the line.

Frequently Asked Questions About Identifying Cockroaches

What does a cockroach look like to the naked eye?

A cockroach looks like a flat, oval, brown or black insect with long waving antennae, six spiny legs and a shield that hides its head from above. Most adults have leathery wings folded flat on the back. They run fast and head straight for cracks when a light turns on.

Do cockroaches bite?

Bites are rare. Cockroaches can bite in heavy infestations, but they are much more of a contamination and allergy concern than a biting pest. Our post on whether cockroaches bite covers the details.

Is one cockroach a sign of an infestation?

One large American or Turkestan roach is often a visitor from outside. One small German roach, a nymph, or an egg case indoors usually means a breeding population, because German roaches rarely live alone.

What is the difference between a palmetto bug and a cockroach?

There isn't one in Arizona. "Palmetto bug" and "water bug" are nicknames for large cockroaches, usually the American cockroach. They are the same insect with a friendlier name.

Why do I only see cockroaches at night?

Roaches avoid light and come out to feed after dark. Seeing them during the day, especially German roaches, often means hiding spots are full and the population is large.

When should I call a professional?

Call us if you see small tan roaches indoors, find egg cases or nymphs, or keep seeing large roaches come up through drains. You can request service online or call our Phoenix-area team at (480) 422-8388. If you want more neighborhood-specific advice, our Ocotillo roach guide covers prevention for southern Chandler homes.

do-termites-fly-what-apache-junction-hom.title: Do Termites Fly? What Apache Junction Homeowners Should Know About Termite Swarmers
do-termites-fly-what-apache-junction-hom.excerpt: Yes, but only swarmers fly, briefly, after rain. How Apache Junction homeowners can tell flying termites from ants, and what a swarm means for the house.
do-termites-fly-what-apache-junction-hom.content:
Yes, termites fly, but only one kind of termite and only for a few minutes of its life. The winged termites you see are swarmers, young kings and queens that leave a mature colony to start a new one. Workers, the termites that chew and eat the wood, and soldiers, which guard the colony, never grow wings. Around Apache Junction, swarmers usually take off after rain. If they show up inside your house, call (480) 422-8388 for an inspection.

We get this question a lot from homeowners in 85119 and 85120, usually right after a storm rolls off the Superstition Mountains and a cloud of winged insects shows up on the patio light. Most people want to know two things. Was that termites? And does it mean termites are in my house? This guide answers both. It covers which termites fly, when they fly in Pinal County, how to tell a flying termite from a flying ant, and what to do in the first hour after a swarm. When you need it, our termite treatment in Apache Junction picks up where this guide leaves off.

Do All Termites Have Wings?

No. A termite colony has three castes, and only one of them ever flies:

  • Workers are soft, pale and wingless. They make up most of the colony, chew the wood and build the mud tubes you see on stem walls and block fences. These are the termites that do the damage.
  • Soldiers are also wingless. They have larger, darker heads and strong jaws for guarding the colony from ants.
  • Reproductives (alates, or swarmers) are the only termites with wings. They are darker than workers, with fully formed eyes and two pairs of long wings. A colony usually has to be a few years old before it starts producing them.

So when someone asks "do termites fly?", the honest answer is that the colony sends out flyers once in a while. The termites eating a house stay underground or inside the wood the whole time.

Why Do Termites Fly at All?

Flying is how termites start new colonies. Once a year or so, a mature colony releases swarmers, often thousands at once. They flutter up, drift a short distance, land, and break off their own wings. Then a male and female pair up, look for moist soil or wood, and seal themselves in to become the king and queen of a new colony.

Termites are weak fliers. Most swarmers travel only a short distance, often helped by the breeze, and the flight itself is over in minutes. Birds, lizards, ants and the Arizona sun kill the large majority of them before they ever find a place to nest. That is why a swarm does not mean thousands of new colonies. What it does tell you is that a mature colony is close by.

How long do flying termites live?

Not long once they leave the nest. A swarmer that does not find a mate and a moist spot quickly dries out and dies, usually within a day. Indoors, swarmers head for windows and lights and die on the sills. That is why piles of dead termites and loose wings near a window are one of the most common signs we find.

When Do Termites Swarm in Apache Junction?

Timing depends on the species. Rain is the biggest trigger here, because swarmers need damp soil to dig into after they land. These are the patterns we see across the East Valley and Pinal County:

TermiteHow common hereTypical swarm seasonTime of dayWhat you usually notice
Desert subterranean termite (Heterotermes aureus)The most common structural termite in the low desertSummer monsoon, July into September, after stormsDusk and after darkSmall pale-yellow to tan swarmers around porch lights and windows on humid evenings
Arid-land subterranean termite (Reticulitermes)Common across ArizonaLate winter and spring, after rainDaytime, often on warm, sunny daysDark brown to black swarmers coming out of soil, a stem wall crack or a slab joint
Desert or tube-building termites (Gnathamitermes and relatives)Very common in open desert and yardsAfter summer rainsDaytime and eveningSwarmers over open ground; mud casings on dead plants and wood mulch rather than on the house
Drywood termitesLess common in our area than subterranean termitesLate summer and fallOften at night, drawn to lightsSwarmers indoors plus tiny, hard, six-sided pellets below wood trim or furniture

Ranges and dates vary by year and by how much rain falls. The University of Arizona's Cooperative Extension and UC IPM's termite pest note cover these species in more detail. In practice, we hear from Apache Junction homeowners most after the first big monsoon storms of summer and again after winter and spring storms. A swarm in November is less common, but a warm stretch after a fall rain can still set one off.

Is It a Flying Termite or a Flying Ant?

This is the question that matters most, because flying ants are harmless to your house in most cases and flying termites are not. Carpenter ants and several desert ants swarm at the same times of year. Check three things, ideally on an insect you have caught in a zip bag or on a piece of clear tape:

  1. The waist. A termite's body is thick and straight from front to back. An ant has a pinched, wasp-like waist.
  2. The antennae. Termite antennae are straight and look like a string of tiny beads. Ant antennae bend in the middle like an elbow.
  3. The wings. A termite's four wings are all about the same length and stretch well past the end of its body. They fall off easily. An ant's front wings are clearly longer than the back pair.

Our Phoenix guide to termites that look like flying ants has more detail on telling them apart. If you have already found wingless, cream-colored insects, our Mesa guide to what termites look like will help you match them.

Does Seeing Flying Termites Mean My House Is Infested?

Not always, but where you see them tells you a lot.

Swarmers outside, in the yard or on a fence

A swarm coming out of the ground in the yard, a dead mesquite stump, an old railroad tie or a pile of firewood means there is a colony in the yard. That is common in Apache Junction, where many lots back onto open desert near the Superstition Wilderness and the washes that run off it. It does not prove the house is infested. It does mean termites are close, and subterranean termites forage a long way underground. That is a good time to book an inspection.

Swarmers inside the house

Swarmers indoors are a much stronger sign. Swarmers come out where the colony is. If they are emerging from a baseboard, a bathroom floor, a slab crack, a garage stem wall or a window frame, the colony is very likely under or inside the structure. Dead swarmers and shed wings on windowsills, in light fixtures or in spider webs in the garage point the same way. We treat this as a call-us-this-week situation.

Do flying termites bite or hurt people?

No. Swarmers do not bite, sting or carry disease. The only risk is to your house, and that risk comes from the colony that sent them out.

What Should I Do Right After a Termite Swarm?

Swarms look alarming, but you have time to do this right. Termite damage builds over months and years, not hours. Here is what we tell homeowners on the phone:

  • Save a few samples. Put several insects and some wings in a zip bag or on clear tape. It makes identification fast and certain.
  • Note where they came from. A window, a slab crack, a wall outlet or a garage corner. Take a photo if you can.
  • Vacuum up the rest. Swarmers indoors will die on their own. A store-bought aerosol kills the swarmers you can see but does nothing to the colony.
  • Leave mud tubes alone. If you find pencil-width mud tubes on the foundation, don't scrape them off before an inspection. They show where termites are traveling.
  • Check for moisture. Leaky irrigation, a dripping AC condensate line or a downspout dumping water against the foundation makes the soil there more attractive to termites.
  • Book an inspection. A trained inspector can confirm the species, find the entry points and recommend a plan.

Why Are Apache Junction Homes Prone to Termites?

We are based here at 2073 W Houston Ave, so we see the same patterns on job after job, and our post on termite treatment for Goldfield Ranch homes walks through a few of them. A few local conditions keep termite pressure high:

  • Open desert on every side. Native termite colonies live in the soil under the creosote and palo verde across Apache Junction, Gold Canyon and the land around Lost Dutchman State Park. New lots and older homes alike sit right next to them.
  • Monsoon storms off the Superstitions. Summer storms soak the ground in a hurry. That is exactly the cue desert subterranean termites wait for.
  • A wide mix of housing. Older site-built homes, manufactured homes, and newer builds along the Apache Trail and in the Superstition Foothills each have their own weak spots, from wood skirting and stem walls to slab joints and plumbing penetrations.
  • Wood in contact with soil. Fence posts, landscape timbers, wood mulch and stacked firewood give foraging termites an easy food source near the house.

How Do We Treat Termites After a Swarm?

Killing swarmers is not the goal. The goal is to protect the house from the colony that produced them. After an inspection, we recommend one of two proven approaches, or both together:

  • Liquid soil treatment. We apply a non-repellent termiticide (Termidor) into the soil along the foundation and at key entry points. Termites that pass through it pick it up and carry it back to the colony.
  • Baiting. Sentricon bait stations go in the soil around the home. Foraging workers find the bait and share it through the colony.

Every treatment includes a warranty and an annual re-inspection. If you bought a new build and the builder used us for the pre-construction treatment, register your warranty so the coverage stays active. You can see the full process on our Apache Junction pest control page, where termite work sits alongside our scorpion and rodent programs.

Do you serve nearby communities too?

Yes. The same swarm seasons and species run across the eastern edge of the Valley. We do termite control in Gold Canyon, termite treatment in San Tan Valley, termite treatment in Queen Creek and termite treatment in Mesa. Farther south, our pest control in Florence covers Anthem at Merrill Ranch and Magic Ranch. For a deeper look at treatment choices, read our Avondale guide on how to get rid of subterranean termites.

Frequently Asked Questions About Flying Termites

Do termites fly at night?

Some do. In our area, desert subterranean termites usually swarm around dusk and after dark during the monsoon, and drywood termites often fly at night toward lights. Arid-land subterranean termites tend to swarm during the day in late winter and spring.

Why do flying termites come to lights?

Swarmers are drawn to light, which normally helps them leave the nest and get into open air. Indoors, it pulls them to windows, lamps and light fixtures, where they usually die. Turning off porch lights on muggy monsoon evenings cuts down how many end up around your doors.

How long does a termite swarm last?

The flight itself is usually over within an hour, and often much faster. A colony can release more than one swarm over several days or weeks of the season, so seeing a second wave does not mean a second colony.

Can flying termites damage furniture?

Swarmers don't eat wood. Workers do the damage. Drywood termites can live inside furniture and trim, though, and swarmers coming out of a piece of wood furniture along with small pellets is a sign of drywood termites in that piece.

Will termite swarmers go away on their own?

The swarmers will. They die within hours to a day if they cannot find soil or wood. The colony that sent them out does not go away, which is why an inspection matters more than cleanup.

how-to-get-rid-of-crickets-what-florence.title: How to Get Rid of Crickets: What Florence Homeowners Should Know Before They Draw In Scorpions
how-to-get-rid-of-crickets-what-florence.excerpt: Cut the lights and moisture that draw crickets, trap the ones inside and treat the perimeter. Why it matters in Florence, where crickets feed scorpions.
how-to-get-rid-of-crickets-what-florence.content:
To get rid of crickets, cut off what draws them to your house (bright lights at night, damp soil at the foundation and gaps under doors), catch the ones inside with sticky traps and a vacuum, and treat the outside perimeter. In Florence it matters more, because crickets feed bark scorpions. If they keep coming back, call (480) 422-8388.

Florence homeowners in 85132 usually notice crickets the same way: one chirping behind the washer that nobody can find, then a dozen dead ones in the garage, then a scorpion in the hallway a week later. This guide explains why crickets end up inside, how to clear them out, and how to keep them from coming back. It also explains the link to scorpions, which is the part most cricket articles skip. When the crickets are a sign of a bigger bug problem, our pest control in Florence treats the whole perimeter, not just the hallway.

Why Do Crickets Show Up Around Florence Homes?

Crickets come inside for shelter and moisture, and they find your house because of light. They hide during the day and move at night. UC IPM, the University of California's pest program, notes that crickets need shelter during the day and often move in from weedy areas as those areas dry out (UC IPM: Crickets).

Florence has a lot of that kind of edge. Here is what our technicians typically see around town:

  • Farm fields and open desert next to neighborhoods. Much of Florence borders irrigated fields and open desert. When a field is cut or a weedy lot dries out, the insects living in it go looking for the next damp, shaded spot, and a block wall or garage door is often the closest one.
  • The Gila River corridor. Older homes near Historic Florence and along the river sit close to brush and damp ground that holds insects through the summer.
  • New-build lighting. In Anthem at Merrill Ranch and Magic Ranch, rows of bright coach lights and garage lights on new homes act like beacons on warm nights. Crickets fly or hop toward the light and then slip under the nearest door.
  • Drip lines and gravel. Irrigation that keeps soil wet along the foundation gives crickets the moisture they need, and gravel beds give them cover.

What Kind of Crickets Are in My House?

Most crickets inside Florence homes are field crickets that wandered in from outside. Telling them apart helps you judge how big the problem really is.

Field crickets

Field crickets are shiny black or dark brown, about 0.6 to 1 inch long, with long antennae, which matches UC IPM's description. These are the loud ones. They live outdoors and usually don't build a lasting population inside a house, so a few in the garage often means they are coming in from outside, not breeding indoors.

House crickets

House crickets are lighter, a tan or straw color, with dark bands across the head. They tolerate indoor life better than field crickets and can keep going in warm, cluttered spaces like garages, laundry rooms and storage closets.

Crickets vs. other jumping bugs

Homeowners sometimes call any jumping insect a cricket. If what you're seeing is small, dark and hanging around a pet's bedding, it may be fleas instead. If it's large, pale and bulbous, it may be a Jerusalem cricket, which isn't a true cricket and rarely comes inside. When you aren't sure, a clear photo helps our team tell you what you're dealing with before a visit.

Do Crickets Attract Scorpions?

Yes. Crickets are one of the main foods for Arizona bark scorpions, so a yard full of crickets can feed scorpions near your walls. Bark scorpions hunt at night, and they go where the prey is. A cricket problem along the foundation tends to bring scorpions with it.

That is the main reason we don't treat crickets as a nuisance-only pest in Pinal County. When our technicians find heavy cricket activity along a block wall, we also look for scorpion harborage: stacked pavers, wood piles, gaps at the bottom of stucco and loose weatherstripping. If you are already seeing scorpions, read our guide to what bark scorpions eat and what draws them indoors, and look at scorpion control in Florence. Cutting down the crickets is one of the first steps in scorpion prevention.

Spiders follow the same food chain. Black widows build webs low on walls and in garage corners where crickets travel, which is why our spider prevention guide for Florence homes also talks about lighting and door gaps.

How Do You Get Rid of Crickets in the House?

Catch what's inside, then close the doors they used to get in. Spraying a few crickets you can see won't fix much if new ones keep coming under the door every night. Here is the order we recommend:

  1. Vacuum the ones you can see. A vacuum picks up live crickets, dead crickets and any eggs in corners. Empty the canister outside.
  2. Set sticky traps (glue boards). Put them along walls in the garage, laundry room and behind appliances, where crickets travel at night. Keep them away from pets and small children. Check them after a few nights. The traps also tell you where the crickets are coming in.
  3. Find the chirper by sound. Crickets go quiet when you get close. Walk slowly, stop, and wait for the chirp to start again. They are usually under a washer, behind a water heater closet door or in a box on the garage floor.
  4. Dry things out. Fix leaks under sinks and at the water heater, and run a fan in damp laundry rooms. Crickets don't last long in dry indoor air.
  5. Clear the floor clutter. Cardboard boxes, stored clothes and piles of shoes give crickets cover. Field crickets may also chew fabric, especially soiled fabric, so get stored clothing off the garage floor.
  6. Seal where they came in. Look at the bottom of garage doors, door sweeps, gaps around plumbing under sinks and any cracks at the base of the wall. Replace worn weatherstripping and add door sweeps.

How Do You Keep Crickets Away From the Outside of Your Home?

Make the area right around the house dark, dry and bare. Crickets that never reach the wall can't get under the door.

  • Change the lights. Swap bright white porch and garage bulbs for yellow "bug light" bulbs, or put them on motion sensors. Point floodlights away from the house so insects gather out in the yard, not at your door.
  • Keep the foundation dry. Adjust drip emitters and sprinklers so they don't soak the strip of soil and gravel against the wall. Fix leaky hose bibs.
  • Clear a gap along the wall. Move wood piles, stored pavers, potted plants and yard debris away from the foundation. Pull weeds along the wall and fence line, where crickets hide during the day.
  • Close the garage at night. An open garage with the light on is one of the easiest ways for crickets to get in on a summer evening.
  • Treat the perimeter. A professional perimeter treatment around the foundation, door thresholds and block wall joints stops many crickets before they reach the door. This is the same band we treat for scorpions, ants and roaches.

When Are Crickets Worst in Arizona?

Summer and the monsoon are the peak, and winter is the quiet season. Arizona search interest shows the same pattern. The table below uses Google search volume for "how to get rid of crickets" in Arizona (DataForSEO, pulled November 18, 2026), next to what our technicians usually see in the field.

March to May320 to 590Activity picks up as nights warm; a good time to seal and adjust lighting
June to August1,600 to 1,900Peak season; heavy numbers at lights and garage doors, especially around monsoon storms
September to November260 to 1,300Numbers taper off as nights cool; crickets look for sheltered spots near the house

The practical lesson: the best time to prevent next summer's crickets is spring, before the population builds. Sealing doors and changing bulbs in March costs you an afternoon. Waiting until July means fighting them at the door every night.

Which DIY Cricket Remedies Actually Work?

Some home remedies help with a few crickets indoors. None of them stop a steady stream from outside. Here's an honest look at the common ones:

Call when crickets keep showing up after you've sealed doors and fixed the lighting, or when you're also seeing scorpions, spiders or roaches. Steady crickets usually mean the area around the house is feeding other pests too.

When our technicians come out, we walk the outside of the house first. We look at lighting, irrigation, door seals, block wall joints and the gravel along the foundation. Then we treat the perimeter and entry points and point out anything that is pulling crickets toward the house. Frequently Asked Questions About Crickets in Florence Homes

Why are there so many crickets in my house all of a sudden?

A sudden wave usually means something changed outside: a nearby field or weedy lot dried out, a monsoon storm passed through, or the nights warmed up. Crickets head for light and moisture, and an open garage or worn door sweep lets them in. Check your lighting and door seals first.

Do crickets attract scorpions?

Yes. Bark scorpions eat crickets and hunt where crickets gather. Reducing crickets along the foundation is one of the most useful things you can do to cut down scorpion activity around a Florence home.

What kills crickets fast?

Vacuuming removes the ones you can see right away, and sticky traps catch the ones that move at night. For crickets coming in from outside, a professional perimeter treatment, darker lighting and sealed doors do more than any quick fix.

Do crickets bite or damage anything?

Crickets aren't known to bite people in any meaningful way, and they don't spread disease. Field crickets can chew fabric, especially soiled clothing, and paper stored on the floor. The bigger concern in Arizona is the scorpions and spiders that feed on them.

How long will a cricket live in my house?

Field crickets usually don't survive long indoors, especially in dry, air-conditioned rooms. House crickets can last longer in warm, cluttered spaces like garages. If crickets keep showing up, they're most likely still coming in from outside.

Start with the steps in this guide: change the lights, dry the foundation, seal doors and trap the ones inside. If they keep coming, call our Phoenix-area team at (480) 422-8388 or request service online and we'll treat the perimeter and check for scorpions while we're there.

what-are-harvester-ants-what-queen-creek.title: What Are Harvester Ants? What Queen Creek Homeowners Should Know About Bare Dirt Circles and Painful Stings
what-are-harvester-ants-what-queen-creek.excerpt: Harvester ants are big seed-eating desert ants that clear bare dirt circles and sting hard. How to identify them in Queen Creek and when to treat the nest.
what-are-harvester-ants-what-queen-creek.content:
Harvester ants are large red, orange, brown or black desert ants (about ¼ to ½ inch long) that collect seeds and clear a bare circle of dirt around their nest. They don't damage houses, but they sting hard and defend the nest aggressively. In a Queen Creek yard where kids or pets play, treat the nest with a labeled bait or call (480) 422-8388.

Most Queen Creek homeowners meet harvester ants the same way. A bald patch of dirt shows up in the gravel, with a low mound of tiny pebbles in the middle and a steady line of big reddish ants carrying seeds into a hole. Then somebody kneels down to pull a weed near it, or the dog noses the mound, and finds out how much the sting hurts. This guide covers how to tell harvester ants apart from other Arizona ants, when they actually need treatment, and what works on them. Most DIY ant products are made for sugar ants, and harvester ants eat something else. For the ants that come inside or nest against the foundation, our ant control in Queen Creek treats both the nests and the perimeter.

What Do Harvester Ants Look Like?

Harvester ants are some of the biggest ants you'll see in an East Valley yard. According to the University of Arizona Cooperative Extension, workers are usually ¼ to ½ inch long and range from orange and red to brown or black. Several of the 22 U.S. species live in Arizona (UA Cooperative Extension: Harvester Ants).

The nest gives them away more than the ant does. Look for these signs:

  • A bare, roughly circular patch. Workers strip the vegetation around the entrance. Out in open desert these circles can reach 35 feet across. In a landscaped Queen Creek yard they're usually a few feet wide because irrigation, rock and pavers get in the way.
  • A low mound of fine gravel. Many species pile tiny pebbles around the entrance, sometimes mixed with bits of charcoal and dead plant material.
  • One to three entrance holes. The extension notes nests are commonly about three feet deep.
  • Seed traffic. Workers walk out alone or along scent trails and come back carrying seeds. They often gather one kind of seed until it runs out, then switch.
  • Midday quiet. Harvester ants are least active during the hottest part of the day, so the mound can look abandoned at 2 p.m. in July and busy again in the evening.

Is it a harvester ant or a fire ant?

Arizona's native fire ants are smaller, reddish-brown ants of mixed sizes that swarm out of loose soil when disturbed. Harvester ants are bigger, all about the same size in a given nest, and build that telltale cleared circle. The table below covers the ants Queen Creek homeowners mix up most often.

AntSize and colorNest signWhat it eatsMain problem
Harvester ant¼–½ in.; orange, red, brown or blackBare circle with a pebble mound in the middleMostly seeds, some insectsPainful sting near the nest
Native fire antSmall, mixed sizes; reddish-brownLoose soil, often along sidewalks and irrigation linesInsects, greasy and protein foodsSwarming stings when disturbed
Sugar ants (several small species)Tiny; black or brownHidden under pavers, in wall voids, near waterSweets, honeydewTrails inside kitchens and bathrooms
Carpenter antLarge; black or red-and-blackSawdust-like debris near damp woodInsects, sweetsNesting in moist or rotted wood

Do Harvester Ants Sting, and How Bad Is It?

Yes. Harvester ants sting, and they will aggressively defend the nest when it's disturbed. The University of Arizona extension warns that people with insect-sting allergies should be especially careful, and notes that some species have barbed stingers that pull out in the skin, the way a honeybee's does. Most people describe the sting as sharp and long-lasting compared with other ants.

One of the species found in the low deserts around Phoenix is the Maricopa harvester ant (Pogonomyrmex maricopa). Insect venom researchers rank its venom among the most toxic of any insect tested. That doesn't mean one sting is dangerous to a healthy adult; the dose from a single ant is tiny. It does mean a mound next to a play area or a dog run deserves attention.

What to do after a sting:

  1. Move away from the mound so you don't collect more stings.
  2. Wash the spot with soap and water and use a cold pack for the pain and swelling.
  3. Watch for signs of a severe allergic reaction: trouble breathing, swelling of the face, lips or throat, hives spreading across the body, or dizziness. Call 911 if any appear.
  4. For a pet that was stung many times or seems weak or swollen, call your veterinarian.

Why Are Harvester Ants So Common in Queen Creek Yards?

Queen Creek was farmland and open desert not long ago, and harvester ants were here first. Our technicians see the most nests in three kinds of places around 85140 and 85142:

  • Lots that back onto open desert. Homes on the south and east edges of town, toward San Tan Mountain Regional Park, border undisturbed desert where colonies are already established. New colonies spread into the closest bare, sunny ground, which is often a back yard.
  • Acreage and horse properties. Around the Horseshoe Park and Equestrian Centre area and the larger lots off Ellsworth and Rittenhouse, wide gravel areas and seed from feed and weeds give harvester ants everything they need.
  • Newer neighborhoods with fresh decomposed granite. In communities like Hastings Farms and Ironwood Crossing, freshly graded yards with sparse plants are exactly the open, sunny ground new queens look for.

Weeds feed them, too. Harvester ants live on seeds, so a yard with spurge, grasses and other seeding weeds is a pantry. Keeping weeds from going to seed is one of the quiet ways to make a yard less attractive to them.

When Do Harvester Ants Swarm and Start New Nests?

In Arizona, winged male and female harvester ants fly, mate and start new nests in spring or summer, usually after a rain. The males die after mating. The new queen drops her wings, digs a burrow and lays her first eggs, and a queen can keep a colony going for years. That's why the same yard can see a new mound appear after the monsoon even when last year's nest was treated.

MonthArizona searchesWhat we see in Queen Creek yards

Do You Need to Get Rid of Harvester Ants?

Not always, and that surprises people. The University of Arizona extension calls harvester ants a useful part of the desert: they spread seed, loosen the soil and feed other animals. Horned lizards depend on them, and harvester ants can make up as much as 90% of a horned lizard's diet. The extension's advice is to leave a nest alone if it's in a quiet corner of the property, and to treat only nests that put people or pets at risk.

In practice, here's how we'd decide in a Queen Creek yard:

  • Treat it: nests in or next to a play area, dog run, pool deck, patio, walkway, garden bed you work in, or along the foundation; anyone in the house with a sting allergy.
  • Probably leave it: a nest at the far edge of an acreage lot or in a desert strip nobody walks through.
  • Get help: several nests, nests that come back after treatment, or ants getting into the house along with other pests.

How Do You Get Rid of Harvester Ants Without Getting Stung?

Use a bait that the label says is for harvester ants, put it where the foragers will find it, and give it time. The extension names hydramethylnon as the most common active ingredient in these baits. Foragers carry the bait back to the nest, where it reaches the rest of the colony and the queen. Here's the approach that works:

  1. Read the label first. Make sure it lists harvester ants and the site you're treating (lawn, landscape, driveway). The label sets the amount, placement and how long kids and pets stay off the area.
  2. Find the trails. Watch the mound in the morning to see which direction the workers travel, and place the bait along those routes and around the cleared area, not dumped into the hole.
  3. Don't disturb the mound. Raking, digging or watering the nest makes the ants move the colony or stop foraging, and it gets you stung.
  4. Keep the bait dry. Skip a day when sprinklers or rain will soak the area.
  5. Be patient. Baits take time to reach the whole colony. Check activity again in a week or two before deciding it didn't work.

Why don't sugar baits and sprays work on harvester ants?

Harvester ants are seed eaters, so sweet baits made for kitchen ants usually aren't the food they're looking for. That's the same reason a borax-and-sugar mix that sometimes works on sugar ants does little here; we explain that bait in our post on whether borax and sugar kill ants. A surface spray kills the workers you hit, but the queen is several feet underground and keeps laying eggs. Our post on why store-bought ant sprays fail in Queen Creek goes into that in more detail.

What should you never pour on an ant mound?

Don't use gasoline, bleach, boiling water near plants, or mixes of household chemicals. They're dangerous to you and your pets, they can poison the soil around your plants, and they often just push the colony to dig a new entrance a few feet away.

What Does Professional Harvester Ant Control Look Like?

When we treat harvester ants at a Queen Creek home, we start by walking the whole yard, because one obvious mound often has company along the back wall or in the side yard. Our technicians identify the ant first, since the right product for harvester ants is different from what works on fire ants or the small ants trailing into the kitchen. Then we treat the active nests with products labeled for harvester ants and look at the perimeter for any other ants or pests getting into the house.

Because harvester ants usually show up alongside other desert pests, most Queen Creek homeowners pair ant treatment with regular pest control in Queen Creek. Your technician tells you how long to keep kids and pets off treated areas for the product used. If you're also seeing scorpions near those same block walls, our scorpion control in Queen Creek covers the walls, weep screeds and door gaps where both pests come in. Our earlier guide on scorpion control for Hastings Farms homeowners explains that side of it.

Do Harvester Ants Get Into Houses?

Rarely. Harvester ants live outdoors and don't nest in walls or eat household food. When a homeowner finds ants inside, it's usually a smaller species following moisture or sweets. If you have both problems, the outdoor harvester ants and the ants in the pantry need different treatments. Our ant elimination guide for Gilbert homeowners covers the indoor kinds we see most across the East Valley.

Do We Treat Harvester Ants in Nearby Cities Too?

Yes. Our Phoenix-area team covers Queen Creek and the communities around it, including San Tan Valley, Gilbert, Mesa, Florence and Apache Junction. San Tan Valley has the same desert-edge neighborhoods off Hunt Highway, and our pest control in San Tan Valley sees plenty of harvester ant mounds in new-build gravel yards. To the north, pest control in Mesa covers the east Mesa neighborhoods near the Superstitions, and our pest control in Apache Junction team works right at the base of the mountains, where colonies are everywhere. You can find everything we do locally on our Queen Creek services page.

Frequently Asked Questions About Harvester Ants in Queen Creek

Are harvester ants dangerous?

They're not dangerous to your house, but their sting is painful, and they defend the nest aggressively. People with insect-sting allergies should take them seriously. A nest near a play area, pool deck or dog run is worth treating.

Why is there a bare circle of dirt in my yard?

That's almost always a harvester ant nest. Workers clear the plants around the entrance and often build a low mound of fine gravel in the middle. Look for large reddish or dark ants carrying seeds in and out of a hole.

Should I leave harvester ants alone?

If the nest is in a far corner of the property that nobody uses, the University of Arizona extension suggests leaving it, since harvester ants help the desert and feed horned lizards. Treat nests that are close to people or pets.

What is the best way to kill harvester ants?

A bait labeled for harvester ants, placed along the foraging trails and around the cleared area, works better than sprays. The workers carry it into the nest and it reaches the queen. Follow the label and give it a week or two.

Do harvester ants come back after treatment?

A treated colony usually doesn't, but new queens fly after spring and monsoon rains and can start a new nest nearby. Yards next to open desert see new mounds more often, so it's worth checking each summer.

How do I get rid of harvester ants in Queen Creek, AZ?

Start with the steps in this guide. If the nest is close to where your family or pets spend time, or the ants keep coming back, call our Phoenix-area team at (480) 422-8388 or request service online. We'll identify the ant, treat the nests and check the rest of the yard while we're there.
